problem: Learned floor-affordance (robot base placement) predictors for mobile manipulation encode whole-scene point clouds, so irrelevant context and arbitrary target orientations make representations ambiguous. They also train heterogeneous manipulation skills jointly, which entangles shared and task-specific knowledge. Existing benchmarks only cover front-view observations.
motivation: Mobile manipulation needs base placements that maximize downstream manipulation success, not just navigation feasibility. FloAff is mainly determined by local interaction geometry around the target, so it is a target-conditioned local reasoning problem. Different skills nonetheless share spatial requirements such as reachability, visibility and collision-free execution.
key_idea: Crop the point cloud around the target and rotate it into a canonical target-facing frame (CFAR), then train FloAff first on pick-and-place and progressively adapt to door and drawer skills with feature distillation (PFAL).
insight: The ablations show both parts matter. On the harder Layouts benchmark, removing cropping (PCC 0.552 vs 0.738) or orientation alignment (0.683) hurts the most; on MoMa-Kitchen, removing SDL or feature distillation hurts most (PCC 0.707 and 0.729 vs 0.796), while cropping matters little there. Single-task results show CFAR alone gives large gains on orientation-sensitive articulated tasks (OpenSD, CloseDD), and the multi-task results show PFAL's progressive transfer keeps front and side views balanced (0.85 vs 0.85). Baselines such as N2M degrade sharply from front to side view.
method: CFAR crop: keep only points within a sphere of radius r (1.3 m on Styles, 1.2 m on Layouts) around the target position to remove irrelevant scene context.

CFAR orientation alignment: rotate the cropped cloud about the vertical axis by (pi - target yaw) so the target front faces -y. Yaw comes from simulator labels in training and from AxisNet at inference.

AxisNet: a lightweight PointNet-style network that takes the cropped points plus target-object feature and predicts a normalized (sin, cos) yaw vector. It is trained with MSE and yaw augmentation of ±90°, then frozen.
Shared prior learning: train the FloAff predictor on pick-and-place (PnPC2C) as the foundation task, with loss MSE + beta*Soft Dice.

Progressive adaptation: initialize from the pick-and-place model, then jointly fine-tune on OpenSingleDoor, CloseDoubleDoor and CloseDrawer with a feature-distillation loss (lambda=1) against the previous-stage feature extractor.

FloAff-Kitchen benchmark: built in RoboCasa with 4 tasks, Styles and Layouts splits, and front and side views. Labels come from rollouts of a pretrained Diffusion Policy at candidate base poses, with Gaussian smoothing; 24,782 RGB-D samples.

setting.backbone: Point-cloud FloAff prediction network (NavAff-style) with CFAR preprocessing, plus a PointNet-style AxisNet, trained from scratch
setting.training_data: MoMa-Kitchen (456 train scenes) and FloAff-Kitchen (5 training scenes per task, 24,782 RGB-D samples in total with rollout-generated FloAff labels)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D back-projected to a target-conditioned point cloud, plus robot proprioceptive state and target object mask
setting.action_space: dense FloAff probability map over the floor plane, used to choose the robot base placement; manipulation is executed by a pretrained diffusion policy
setting.privileged: Target yaw from simulator annotations during training only; at test time, AxisNet-predicted yaw and the target object mask/position are used.

numbers_note: SR values are printed as fractions (0.85) in the paper; kept as printed. Single-task per-skill SR (Table 3) is not included in the numbers list.
results: On MoMa-Kitchen the method reduces RMSE from 0.147 (NavAff) to 0.073 and raises PCC from 0.680 to 0.796. On FloAff-Kitchen, downstream MoMa success reaches 0.85 (Styles) and 0.79 (Layouts) against 0.50 (C2F-Exp) and 0.49 (C2F-Exp) for the best baselines, close to the Oracle's 0.88 and 0.86. Front and side views perform similarly (0.85/0.85 and 0.81/0.77), whereas N2M drops sharply on side views.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulated kitchens with four skills; real-world mobile manipulation is left as future work.
Inference depends on AxisNet's predicted yaw, so orientation errors could propagate; the crop radius is tuned per benchmark (1.3 m vs 1.2 m).
Each test set has only one unseen scene per task, and labels depend on a specific pretrained manipulation policy.
